Let \(C_n\) denote the strict linear order with \(n\) elements. The key fact is:

\[
\text{Duplicator wins the \(r\)-round game on } C_p,C_q
\iff
p=q \text{ or } \min(p,q)\ge 2^r-1.
\]

I will prove this by induction on \(r\).

For \(r=0\), no elements are chosen, so Duplicator always wins. This matches the condition since \(2^0-1=0\).

Assume the statement holds for \(r-1\). Put

\[
T=2^{r-1}-1,
\qquad
2^r-1=2T+1.
\]

First suppose \(p,q\ge 2^r-1\). If Spoiler chooses an element in \(C_p\), say with \(L\) elements to its left and \(R\) to its right, then

\[
L+R=p-1\ge 2T.
\]

So at least one of \(L,R\) is \(\ge T\). Duplicator chooses an element in \(C_q\) so that any side of size \(<T\) is matched exactly, and every other side has size at least \(T\). This is possible because \(q-1\ge 2T\). Then, on each side, the remaining \((r-1)\)-round game is either between equal finite chains or between two chains both of size at least \(T=2^{r-1}-1\). By the induction hypothesis, Duplicator can continue to win. The same argument applies if Spoiler starts in \(C_q\).

Now suppose \(p<q\) and \(p<2^r-1=2T+1\). If \(p<T\), Spoiler already wins in \(r-1\) rounds by induction, hence also in \(r\) rounds. Otherwise \(T\le p\le 2T\). Spoiler plays the \((T+1)\)-st element of the longer order \(C_q\), leaving \(T\) elements on its left.

If Duplicator answers with one of the first \(T\) elements of \(C_p\), then the left intervals have unequal sizes and the smaller has size \(<T\), so Spoiler wins the remaining \(r-1\) rounds by induction.

If Duplicator answers with the \((T+1)\)-st element or later, then the right interval in \(C_p\) has size at most

\[
p-(T+1)\le 2T-(T+1)=T-1<T,
\]

while the corresponding right interval in \(C_q\) is strictly larger. Again Spoiler wins the remaining \(r-1\) rounds by induction.

Thus the characterization is proved.

Now apply it to

\[
|A_m|=2^m,\qquad |B_m|=2^m+1.
\]

For \(r=m\),

\[
2^m\ge 2^m-1=2^r-1,
\]

so Duplicator wins the \(m\)-round game.

For \(r=m+1\),

\[
2^m<2^{m+1}-1=2^r-1,
\]

and the two orders have unequal sizes, so Spoiler wins.

Therefore the least such \(r\) is

\[
\boxed{m+1}.
\]
